articles.text: My grandmother has this saying in Russian: “И это пройдет”. it means, “And this will pass.” She told me this when I had gotten into a fight with my mother. I had been crying to her over the phone. She had asked me if this was a fight that would result in us never talking again, and I had answered her no. My grandmother told me that of course it wasn’t. And she told me that the old Tsar Solomon wore a ring with “И это пройдет” inscribed on it. She said that she thought of the phrase often whenever she felt as if she was stuck in the past and overcome with sadness. And so, I listened to her. I wrote down the saying on my hand. With tears streaming down my eyes I looked at it. In truth it helped. I didn’t stop crying for a while, but it helped me see past the fog clouding my mind, see past the words, and see the forgiveness waiting for me. The saying made me realize that no feeling ever really stays with you forever. Whether it is happiness, sadness, anxiety. Whatever it is, it will always pass. It taught me that there is always light at the end of the tunnel. It taught me that the darkness and uncertainty of the tunnel was nothing to be afraid of. Instead all you have to do is stand up and follow the light out of the tunnel. My grandmother has taught me many skills throughout my life. She has taught me to sew, to cook, to appreciate opera, and to speak better in Russian, but this has been one of the most important by far. It reminded me that she has lived a long time on this planet, that she has learned things from others and some on her own. The saying she told me that day wasn’t just a temporary fix, or something to comfort me, but to really show me that everything does pass. It showed me that fights won’t last, that things will go back to normal eventually. I have no doubt in my mind that what she said to me will stay with me throughout my life. I also believe that the phrase “и это пройдет” is something that everyone could learn from. It is a phrase that can bring hope to those who think there isn’t any. We live in times when hope is all we are left with. A hope for better times ahead, hope for the dark to end. I know now that eventually everything does come to pass, and that there is no reason to hold onto a fleeting feeling. It has also taught me to never overlook a grandmother’s advice.
articles.title: И Это Пройдет (This too will pass)

articles.text: Nominations due by March 18 for 2022 Heritage Trees The City of Piedmont is currently accepting nominations of noteworthy trees in public open spaces for Piedmont’s fifth year of Heritage Tree designation. Members of the community may nominate trees based on their aesthetic, educational, or historical value. The Piedmont Heritage Tree Program was created by City Council in 2018 upon the recommendation of the Park Commission. The designation recognizes and identifies distinctive trees that are noteworthy for their size, species, location, or historical context in city parks and open spaces. To date, 19 trees or groups of trees are recognized as Heritage Trees in Piedmont. Applications for heritage trees are sought each year, and the program encourages residents to visit City parks and open spaces to find trees eligible for Heritage Tree designation. Nominations will be reviewed by a subcommittee of Piedmont Park Commissioners and Public Works staff. The tree or group of trees selected will be announced at the April 6 Park Commission meeting. To nominate a tree or group of trees, visit https://www. piedmont.ca.gov/government/ commissions_ _ _committees/ park_commission /heritage_ tree_program and download the proposal form. Nominations are due by March 18. Heritage Tree map An interactive map of all Piedmont’s heritage trees is available on the city’s website. Each marker includes the tree or group of trees’ species name, location, year inducted, and the resident who nominated it for the program. Park Commission Chair Patty Dunlap created the map, which is powered by Google Maps with populated information that can be accessed on any computer, smartphone or other device. Photos of all trees were taken by Park Commissioner Brian Mahany. The map can be accessed by visiting: https://www.piedmont. ca.gov/gover nment/commissions___committees/park_commission/heritage_tree_program. articles.text: The City of Oakland imposed a proof of vaccination ordinance on Tuesday, February 1, which requires all patrons to show proof of up-to-date COVID vaccinations to enter many indoor facilities, including bars, restaurants, clubs, and gyms. In addition, patrons will be asked to show proof of vaccination to enter senior adult care facilities and city senior programs. To enter Oakland City Hall, you may show proof of vaccination or a recent negative COVID-19 test within 72 hours of entry. Patrons will be expected to show their vaccination status at large, indoor events at city and privately-owned facilities. The vaccination requirements for private and public indoor events are in place for events with 1,000 or more attendees. The ordinance is similar to San Francisco’s ordinance in August 2021 which required businesses in high-contact indoor sectors to verify vaccination status. This does not include shopping establishments, department stores, or grocery stores.
articles.title: Proof of vaccination now required for Oakland restaurants, bars

Scout Executive Kate Benson. “He’s already demonstrated a depth of Scouting knowledge that will be helpful in serving our Scouts and volunteers. articles.text: Writing can take many forms. The key is practice and fun. Reading and writing are fundamental steps in early learning for young children. Often the focus is reading, which is essential for recognizing that pictures represent symbols, building vocabulary and establishing the context of print. Another essential exercise in building those muscles is writing. Writing reinforces reading and vocabulary development. Emerging writers (ages 2-6) are developing the skills by drawing pictures and symbols that mimic writing. Soon they progress to actually putting together words and sentences that begin to communicate real and imagined concepts. Supporting early writing leads to necessary outcomes such as fine motor skills, building the context of print, phonics and creative expression. Below are just a few ways children of all ages can strengthen their literacy muscles: Draw and write Support young learners in expressing their ideas through pictures and/or words. Ask them to tell you a story through pictures, or drawing a story about their day. Using your imagination Ask children to make up a story. Perhaps they can write about a character in one of their favorite books. As they create, ask questions to keep the juices flowing. Be the scribe Ask your child to tell you a story and you be the scribe, writing what they say word-for-word. Asking questions is the key to keep it moving. Encourage variety Perhaps a child is more interested in poems, or jokes or drawings. Writing takes many forms. What engages your young writer? Collaborate Share a notebook with a child or with the whole family. Perhaps everyone has a daily entry. You could all be writing a story together, or talking about your day or introducing new ideas. Supporting children in their writing also supports their ability to tell their stories. At Children’s Fairyland we host a Young Writers workshop in late winter and early spring. Our desire is to make sure young people have a space to hone their writing skills and provide opportunities to tell their own stories. As they do so, they build the necessary muscles for literacy, confidence in storytelling and expand their creativity. Writing can take many forms. The key is practice and fun. Whatever you do to support your young writer will be adding reps (and fun) to their school-day workout. Kymberly Miller is Executive Director at Children’s Fairyland. 699 Bellevue Ave, Oakland, CA 94610. https://fairyland.org/

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. articles.text: Gung Hay Fat Choy (Gong Xi Fa Cai) means “May you be Happy and Prosperous.” Lunar New Year is the longest and most important celebration in Asia, with over 1.5 billion people across the globe celebrating the new year in China, Taiwan, Vietnam, Korea and Singapore for two weeks. Even during the Vietnam war, the Lunar New Year (a holiday called Tet), North and South Vietnamese forces would traditionally call a truce to allow soldiers to return to their families to celebrate. The Chinese year 4720, the Year of the Tiger, began this week on Tuesday, February 1. The Chinese use a 13-month Lunar calendar which explains why Lunar New Year changes every year. The Tiger is the third animal in the Chinese Calendar 12-year cycle. Did you ever wonder how the animals got their order in the Chinese Zodiac? Legend has it that in ancient times Buddha asked all the animals to meet him on Chinese New Year. But only twelve animals came. In order to decide their order in the Chinese Zodiac cycle, the animals held a very exciting race. The first one to cross the river would be granted the first year, the second to come in would be the second animal in the cycle, and so on. The Tiger, being the “King of Beasts”, thought he would win, but did not count on the strong, hardworking Ox which outpaced him. The Tiger ended up third, the Ox came in second, but the clever Rat jumped on the back of the Ox, which did not even feel the little thing getting a free ride. At the last second before reaching shore, the Rat jumped on land, winning the race. The Ox came in second, the Tiger third, and so it went... The happy-go-lucky Pig took his time and came in last, and the Chinese Zodiac and its twelve signs were born. Buddha named a year after each animal and the cycle repeats every 12 years. He announced that the people born in each animal’s year would have some of that animal’s personality. People born in the Year of the Tiger are active and energetic in work. They are bold to accept new things and decisive to take right actions. They are fully devoted in career and long for success. People born in the Year of the A lunar calendar Tiger art installation at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco. Tiger are difficult to resist, for they are magnetic characters and their natural air of authority confers a certain prestige on them. They are tempestuous yet calm, warm-hearted yet fearsome, courageous in the face of danger yet yielding, soft and mysterious. They enjoy a life full of challenges and unexpected events, like visiting unusual places and meeting interesting or outstanding people. Therefore, the most suitable jobs for them are as managers, politicians, actors, police, lawyers, entrepreneurs as well as adventurers. Famous people like Queen Elizabeth II, Sir Richard Branson, Lady Gaga, and adventurer Bear Grylls were born under the year of the Tiger. If you are a tiger, this year you will be either age 12, 24, 36, 48, 60, or 72. Fireworks and Family Feasts At Chinese New Year celebrations people wear red clothes, decorate with poems on red paper, and give children and single people “lucky money” in red envelopes. Red symbolizes fire and good luck, which according to legend can drive away bad luck. The fireworks that shower the festivities also drive away evil spirits. Tangerines and oranges represent prosperity. Families clean their houses, wear new clothes, visit each other, get together for dinner and exchange gifts of food. Year of the Tiger on Parade • The canceled Chinese New Year parade last year left San Francisco with a sudden invention that may end up being an enduring tradition – Lunar New Year zodiac statues installed throughout the city. For the second year in a row, the San Francisco Chinese Chamber of Commerce commissioned a multi-artist Lunar New Year installation public art exhibition, spanning all of the city to ring in the Year of the Tiger. • Six life-sized Tigers will be publicly displayed around San Francisco, from January 17 to February 19 and located in San Francisco’s Chinatown, the Asian Art Museum, Union Square, and Whole Foods at Stonestown Galleria. • The Tiger statues spotlight local artists as well as reflect upon the culture, people, and traditions surrounding Chinese New Year. articles.text: In 2008, the Lantern Festival was listed as an intangible cultural heritage element. The Chinese New Year holiday comes to its climax with the Yuan Xiao (元宵节 / yuán xiāo jié), or Lantern Festival, celebrated on February 15th, 2022. Began over 2000 years ago, the festival has developed many meanings. It celebrates family reunions and society. It features ancient spiritual traditions. Some also call this the “true” Chinese Valentine’s Day. The many activities include moon gazing, lighting lanterns, riddles, lion dances and eating rice balls. According to the lunar calendar, the festival takes place on January 15. Dates of past and future Lantern Festivals using the Gregorian calendar include: 2022: February 15th 2023: February 5th 2024: February 24th 2025: February 12th 2026: March 3rd Cultural Significance of the Lantern Festival The Spring Festival is a time reserved for families. There is the reunion dinner on New Year’s Eve, visits (拜年 / bài nián) to in-laws on the 2nd day and neighbors after that. Stores reopen on the 5th and society basically goes back to normal. But on the 15th, everyone— regardless of age or gender—go out onto the streets to celebrate. Though the Lantern Festival symbolizes reunions (more on that later), it’s also a time of socializing and freedom. In Ancient China, women usually weren’t allowed out the house. But on this night, they can stroll freely, lighting lanterns, playing games and interacting with men. The wild and romantic stories are why some say the Lantern Festival is the true Chinese Valentine’s Day, rather than Qixi (七夕). On a more serious side, the Lantern Festival also has religious aspects. It was important in ancient Chinese paganism, and also modern day Buddhism and ethnic minority cultures. Origins and Histories The general consensus is that the festival began more than 2000 years ago in the Western Han dynasty. Emperor Wu (汉武帝 / hàn wǔ dì) designated this day for worship rituals for Taiyi (太一神 / tài yī shén), one of the universe’s sovereigns. Intense power play and unrest came after his reign. The new emperor was Emperor Wen (汉文 帝 / hàn wén dì). To celebrate the return of peace, he made the 15th a national holiday. Every household would light candles and lanterns. It became known as 闹 元宵 (nào yuán xiāo). “Nao” can be interpreted as having fun, or going wild with excitement. Emperor Ming of the later Eastern Han was a devout Buddhist. He heard that on the 15th, monks would light candles for the Buddha. He ordered the palace and temples to light candles, and for the citizens to hang lanterns. Both events combined and eventually developed into the Lantern Festival we know today. Lantern Festival Celebration The duration of celebrations varied throughout history. Nowadays, the festival technically isn’t a national holiday, so there aren’t any days off. The best period for Lantern Festival lovers would be the Ming dynasty. It lasted around 1 month! There are some holidays that coincide with the Lantern Festival and are now celebrated together. Torch Festival (火把节 / huǒ bǎ jié) The Torch Festival began in ancient times to chase away insects and pests and pray for a good harvest. Children gather firewood and tree branches. Adults then light them. Holding these torches, entire communities dance in fields from dusk to dawn. Even now, it is still celebrated in some parts of Southwestern China. Vegetable Stealing Festival (偷 菜节 / tōu cài jié) This is celebrated by the Miao ethnicity in China. On that day, groups of girls steal Chinese cabbage from someone’s fields. Being caught is totally fine, but it’s forbidden to steal from relatives or friends. Later, everyone puts the stolen Chinese cabbage together to make a feast. The one who eats the most will be the one to marry first. Lighting the Lanterns Lanterns are the most notable part of the festival. Which you can probably tell by the name. In the early days, the Lantern Festival was also called Shang Yuan (上元). It was dedicated to the heavenly palace (天宫 / tiān gōng). People would gather in their yards and give offerings to the gods. The lit lantern near the setup represented a god’s seat. Throughout history, countless variations of lanterns have been created. They can be small globes that fit in your palm, or as large as a parade float. People make lanterns in symbolic designs as well.

Began over 2000 years ago, the festival has developed many meanings. It celebrates family reunions and society. It features ancient spiritual traditions. Some also call this the “true” Chinese Valentine’s Day. The many activities include moon gazing, lighting lanterns, riddles, lion dances and eating rice balls. According to the lunar calendar, the festival takes place on January 15. Dates of past and future Lantern Festivals using the Gregorian calendar include: 2022: February 15th 2023: February 5th 2024: February 24th 2025: February 12th 2026: March 3rd Cultural Significance of the Lantern Festival The Spring Festival is a time reserved for families. There is the reunion dinner on New Year’s Eve, visits (拜年 / bài nián) to in-laws on the 2nd day and neighbors after that. Stores reopen on the 5th and society basically goes back to normal. But on the 15th, everyone— regardless of age or gender—go out onto the streets to celebrate. Though the Lantern Festival symbolizes reunions (more on that later), it’s also a time of socializing and freedom. In Ancient China, women usually weren’t allowed out the house. But on this night, they can stroll freely, lighting lanterns, playing games and interacting with men. The wild and romantic stories are why some say the Lantern Festival is the true Chinese Valentine’s Day, rather than Qixi (七夕). On a more serious side, the Lantern Festival also has religious aspects. It was important in ancient Chinese paganism, and also modern day Buddhism and ethnic minority cultures. Origins and Histories The general consensus is that the festival began more than 2000 years ago in the Western Han dynasty. Emperor Wu (汉武帝 / hàn wǔ dì) designated this day for worship rituals for Taiyi (太一神 / tài yī shén), one of the universe’s sovereigns. Intense power play and unrest came after his reign. The new emperor was Emperor Wen (汉文 帝 / hàn wén dì). To celebrate the return of peace, he made the 15th a national holiday. Every household would light candles and lanterns. It became known as 闹 元宵 (nào yuán xiāo). “Nao” can be interpreted as having fun, or going wild with excitement. Emperor Ming of the later Eastern Han was a devout Buddhist. He heard that on the 15th, monks would light candles for the Buddha. He ordered the palace and temples to light candles, and for the citizens to hang lanterns. Both events combined and eventually developed into the Lantern Festival we know today. Lantern Festival Celebration The duration of celebrations varied throughout history. Nowadays, the festival technically isn’t a national holiday, so there aren’t any days off. The best period for Lantern Festival lovers would be the Ming dynasty. It lasted around 1 month! There are some holidays that coincide with the Lantern Festival and are now celebrated together. Torch Festival (火把节 / huǒ bǎ jié) The Torch Festival began in ancient times to chase away insects and pests and pray for a good harvest. Children gather firewood and tree branches. Adults then light them. Holding these torches, entire communities dance in fields from dusk to dawn. Even now, it is still celebrated in some parts of Southwestern China. Vegetable Stealing Festival (偷 菜节 / tōu cài jié) This is celebrated by the Miao ethnicity in China. On that day, groups of girls steal Chinese cabbage from someone’s fields. Being caught is totally fine, but it’s forbidden to steal from relatives or friends. Later, everyone puts the stolen Chinese cabbage together to make a feast. The one who eats the most will be the one to marry first. Lighting the Lanterns Lanterns are the most notable part of the festival. Which you can probably tell by the name. In the early days, the Lantern Festival was also called Shang Yuan (上元). It was dedicated to the heavenly palace (天宫 / tiān gōng). People would gather in their yards and give offerings to the gods. The lit lantern near the setup represented a god’s seat. Throughout history, countless variations of lanterns have been created. They can be small globes that fit in your palm, or as large as a parade float. People make lanterns in symbolic designs as well. See Lantern Festival on page 11

articles.text: A famous variation is the Kongming lantern (孔明灯 / kǒng míng dēng). They represent hope, success and happiness. In the past, people used these lanterns to signify they were safe after an attack. Now, they are used for wishes. Also known as the sky lantern (天灯 / tiān dēng), it sounds similar to 添丁 (tiān ding), which means “adding children”. Lanterns would be gifted to newlyweds or couples without children to pass on the blessings. Pregnant women would receive a pair of small lanterns to wish health and safety on both mother and child. Some regions also burn lanterns to determine the gender of their future child from the shape of the ashes. Traditions and Activities Every holiday has its own set of activities. There’s more to this festival than lanterns. In the city of Fengyang, swings play a major role. A popular saying there is, “Swing on the Lantern Festival, no aches or pains the entire year.” One of the festival sights in Hebei are the jǐng xíng lā huā (井 陉拉花) performances. Holding fans and parasol-like props, folks dance to the beat of drums. Lantern riddles (猜灯谜 / cāi dēng mí) The ancient Chinese would often get together with some friends, drink wine and write poetry. Plays on words and riddles were a favorite pastime. Jǐng xíng lā huā (井陉拉花) performances are energetic and colorful dances that hundreds crowd around to watch. Modern riddles dangling from red lanterns.

It’s also known as tāng yuan (汤 圆) in the South, and one of the many tasty Chinese New Year desserts. The team remains undefeated against Foothill Division opponents. “It was a great game, great fun, high energy, and a good team performance,” said coach Dan Chubbock after the draw with O’Dowd. “It shows how stronger our team is than last year. articles.text: Piedmont romps past O’Dowd 54-34, Berkeley 63-39 Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team made short work of Bishop O’Dowd on Saturday, January 29, defeating the Dragons 54-34. It marked the team’s second consecutive victory over BOD after closing the shortened spring season in 2021 with a 66-55 win in June. The Highlanders also swatted the Berkeley Yellowjackets 63-39 two days earlier, January 27. The two wins improve Piedmont’s record to 14-4 and puts them in the driver’s seat for the Foothill Division title. But first PHS will need to get by San Leandro to whom they surprisingly lost 50-49 on January 21. O’Dowd struggled with finishing shots, while Piedmont’s defense was instrumental in forcing difficult looks for the Dragon shooters, holding the Dragons to five points in the first quarter and eight in the fourth. “They didn’t shoot it particularly well and our defense was very solid. We used a bit of a zone defense and went from there. It will be an interesting end to the season. If we can continue competing like this, who knows what can happen,” said coach Bryan Gardere. Maddie Hill was electric against Bishop O’Dowd, scoring 17 points with four assists and three steals. Her energy on the floor was a galvanizing presence for the rest of the team. “I wanted to bring a lot of energy and I think that boosted our confidence. It feels great to beat them. O’Dowd has been our rival for over a decade. This game always comes with some pride,” said Hill. Piedmont has won three of the last five games with O’Dowd since a win in 2019. Piedmont has competed in the Foothill Division since 2012 and has competed with BOD for more than 15 years. One member of the team, senior Hannah Govert, has been part of all three victories, putting her in very exclusive company in the school’s history for total wins against its Oakland rivals. Staff Photos \Maddie Hill had 17 points against Bishop O’Dowd and set the tone in Piedmont’s 54-34 win. Hannah Govert now has three wins over Bishop O’Dowd in her high school career. articles.text: Area in San Mateo County includes 1,800-year old Methuselah Tree & prehistoric Tafoni rock formation Photo courtesy of AllTrails The Methusela Tree, estimated to be 1,800 years old, is located near Highway 35 (Skyline Blvd). Previously closed to the public, you can now walk up for your photo-op with the Big Old Tree. El Corte de Madera Creek Preserve in San Mateo County has some easily accessible features that many more acclaimed destinations around the Bay Area don’t come close to offering. Sitting near Highway 35 (Skyline Boulevard) is a tree that predates the Europeans settling in America, the estimated 1,800- year old Methuselah Tree. It is the only old growth redwood tree in the Santa Cruz Mountains outside of Big Basin State Park. It is known by locals as the “Big Old Tree on Skyline.” The Peninsula Open Space Preserve states that the Methuselah Tree sprouted in 217 AD, experienced Ohlone Native’s bark cultivation in 1,000 AD, was witness to European settlers and Mexico’s independence from Spain in 1821, while lumber mills in the 1870s California Gold Rush likely determined that its massive burl made Methuselah impossible to harvest. The last time we visited, in December 2020, the entrance to the tree was closed due to dry conditions. It has since re-opened to the public, making it an excellent place for a photo-op and a starting point for a day of hiking. You can walk up to the Big Old Tree and sit on its stump. Across the road from the Methuselah Tree is the Sierra Morena Trail, the starting point for a 1.5 mile hike to another historic landmark, the Tafoni Rock Formation. The near 40-foot tall hunk of sandstone is an estimated 30 million years old and progressively deteriorating from wind and rain over time. A platform sits at its base with informative panels of its history and a clear view. The rock formation, Tafoni, is a name to describe the sandstone’s cavernous reaction from weathering conditions. You can spot examples of Tafoni formations along the Pacific coast as wind and waves eat away at shorelines. El Corte de Madera’s represents a prehistoric time, dating back to the middle of the Cenozoic Era when the ocean covered San Mateo County. A half-mile away from the rock formation, continuing on the Fir Trail, is another place of note, the Vista Point overlook. It offers has a narrow view of the Pacific Ocean and has a bench for resting. An interesting memorial to an air wreckage in the 1950s sits at the entrance. The memorial was erected in 2006 to commemorate a British Commonwealth Pacific Airlines commercial airplane bound for Sydney, Australia that crashed in the park in October 1953. One can still find pieces of the wreckage on the park’s Resolution Trail. Continuing back to the parking lot rounds out your day at a mellow 3.6 miles. But continuing past the Tafoni Rock Formation on the Tafoni Trail will provide a 5.15-mile day and slightly under 1,000 feet in elevation gain while being surrounded by redwood trees and stumps from old giants. This loop trail is a hidden treasure in comparison to hiking on Mt. Tam. No dogs are allowed in El Corte de Madera Creek Preserve, and the trails are a common for mountain bikers zooming downhill. To access the area, punch in “Methuselah Tree, Redwood City” on your GPS device. This article was updated from its original publication in the Post on December 2, 2020. The Tafoni Trail past the rock formation is more secluded and is littered with stumps of old growth redwoods. The area is popular for mountain bikers, so hikers need to be on the alert.

articles.text: Potter and ceramicist Edith Heath. The Oakland Museum of California opened its highly touted exhibit Edith Heath: A Life in Clay on January 29. The exhibition which celebrates the life and work of the founder of Heath Ceramics, was set to open last year, but was rescheduled due to water damage in the museum during winter rains. A Life in Clay will be on display through October 30. A Life in Clay showcases the legacy of the artist with over 50 pieces of ceramics, clay samples, photographs, and personal memorabilia on display. A documentary video will be shown inside the museum as well. The new exhibition introduces visitors to the artist’s career, which was deeply expressive of California’s land and lifestyle. Heath, who died in 2005, focused on creating dependable and long-lasting products for the home, with a focus on sustainability. The exhibit has been created by Oakland Museum Curator of Photography Drew Johnson, and Photo by Heath Clay Studio guest curator Jennifer Volland. “Edith Heath transformed our notion of ‘good design’ pioneering a new aesthetic of natural, stylish yet functional products made from local materials and designed to endure,” said Johnson. “As an icon of quintessential California design who lived and worked in Sausalito and San Francisco, we are excited to share the extraordinary story of Heath’s life and legacy.” A Life in Clay examines Heath’s technical experimentations with native California clays and glaze formulas. Her love of natural landscapes shaped the quality of her design and inspired her to seek clays from California rather than what was traditionally used for dinnerware. “What began as a rebellion against imported white clay more than 50 years ago is now a modern-day classic,” explained Volland, who has researched the artist since 2014 and served as an essayist for the book Edith Heath: Philosophies. articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre (Berkeley Rep) is performing Swept Away now through March 6 at Peet’s Theatre. San Francisco Ballet will present a selection of three productions and one world premiere at the War Memorial Theatre now through February 12. George Balanchine’s masterful ballet Symphony in C and set to the music of Georges Bizet, will begin the program, with more than 50 San Francisco Ballet dancers onstage. Composer is Peter Ilyich Tchaikovsky’s Trio follows, choreographed by Artistic Director Helgi Tomasson. Dancers will be adorned in billowing gowns and velvet jackets to present the elegant choreography. The world premiere of Mrs. Robinson will complete the program. The newly composed work by Cathy Marston is a nod to the iconic American novella and film The Graduate, this retelling is from the perspective of the titular seductress. “I immediately thought – this is it,” said Marston, after learning the novella is set in San Francisco. “This is the piece that I need to make for San Francisco Ballet.” “In the film, Anne Bancroft is impenetrable,” explained Marston. “And that’s genius, because it means you project your own feelings onto hers. I suppose that was the inspiration for the ballet. I wanted to get underneath the surface and find out why Mrs. Robinson is as she is, why she does the things that she does, and make specific choices based on those answers.” Music for Mrs. Robinson is composed by Terry Davies, with scenic and costume design by Patrick Kinmonth. San Francisco Ballet now requires proof of updated vaccination status to watch live performances. Patrons are also required to wear an N95, KN95, or KF94 mask to enter the venue; the ballet company will provide these masks to patrons if needed. Food and drinks will not be permitted inside the auditorium. There are multiple performance times between February 1 and 12. To see a full list, and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.sf ballet.org/productions/ program-1/. Performances will take place at the San Francisco War Memorial Opera House at 301 Van Ness Avenue across from City Hall. Tickets may also be purchased by calling (415) 865-2000.

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony will open its 50th year with a symphonic concert live in Zellerbach Hall on Sunday afternoon, February 6 at 4 p.m. The opening concert tells a story of rebirth and communal renewal, from Morton Gould’s Protest to Sibelius’ Finlandia to Berkeley composer John Adams’s Lollapalooza. The concert will conclude with Stravinsky’s Firebird Suite, a classic work that celebrates collective reemergence and renewal. Audience members will also enjoy the world premiere of As Water, Freedom by Derrick Skye, a work commissioned by Berkeley Symphony. Skye is a Los Angeles-based composer whose work has been performed by ensembles around the world, including the Los Angeles Chamber Orchestra, Lyris Quartet, Cantori New York, and Super Devoiche Bulgarian Women’s Choir. Artistic Director Rene Mandel explained the change of day and time from the traditional Thursday evening concerts at Zellerbach to Sunday late afternoon. “In an effort to make our conPhoto by Jeff Roman Joseph Young, Conductor for Berkeley Symphony Orchestra certs more accessible to everybody in our community and the entire Bay Area, we made the decision to switch all of our concerts to Sunday matinees,’ he explained. The Symphony’s series of chamber music concerts held at the Piedmont Center for the Arts has been on Sunday afternoons for the past nine years. To purchase tickets, call the box office at (510) 841-2800, ext. 1, visit the website at https:// www.berkeleysymphony.org/ events/symphonic, or e-mail tickets@berkeleysymphony.org.

articles.text: Vin Diesel and Paul Walker reprise their roles in Fast Five, the fifth installment in the Fast and Furious franchise. Fast Five, released in 2011, is a pedal-to-the-metal, rockin’, high octane, high testosterone hottie of a film – perfect for newbie adolescent boys. It uses state of the art film technology to create an experience, a movie in which dialogue is reduced to so much information, used in the main to explain and thus create the next punchy, intense scene. In a franchise which began in 2001 with The Fast and the Furious, this latest incarnation is as good if not better than those that preceded it. Rather than focusing on the chronic gearheads who prowl the backstreets of, say, L.A., driving tricked out rides while setting up match races, Fast Five offers up a nice twist. It borrows heavily from Ocean’s Eleven, and is a flat-out, holdyour-breath heist movie. Yep, there’s ten million bucks stashed in a vault, money that belongs to a kingpin drug dealer, Reyes (Joaquim de Almeida). This ruthless honcho operates out of Rio de Janeiro with its magnificent statue of Christ, arms outstretched as if embracing Rio, with all of its affluence and precariously perched favelas. Brian O’Conner (Paul Walker) and Mia Toretto (Jordana Brewster) are on the lam from the U.S. Federales, hiding out in a favela, waiting for Dom Toretto (Vin Diesel) to arrive. Once he does, the action begins in earnest. Seriously. And just to make sure you’re on board, the opening 20 minutes are a feast of spectacular special effects and very close calls. Of course, you have to suspend your disbelief. The laws of physics play no part in this film. Nor does a tight plot. But no worries, this is pure dash and crash, fast cuts, destruction of tons of property, hand-held cameras capturing some nifty chase scenes, smokin’ hot cars (there’s not a Prius to be found), intense pacing, with only a few moments when director Justin Lin turns down the heat to a simmer for some spare dialogue before stoking the flames once again. Films of this ilk, postmodern types, are not known as talkies. Fast Five was billed as the first film of the summer, and undoubtedly the teen demographic (boys, mostly) will be back in the theaters ready to watch Vin and The Rock, shaved heads gleaming, arms pumped, comparing their hardware, hard stares, and their rides. This franchise pays homage to the growling, rumbling, throaty internal combustion engine like no other. Dude, it’s industrial strength all the way. Fast Five. Directed by Justin Lin. Starring Vin Diesel, Paul Walker, Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson, Jordana Brewster, Joaquim de Almeida. 2 hrs., 30 min. Rated PG-13. This review originally appeared in the Piedmont Post on May 4, 2011.

articles.text: I saw the trailer to The Shape of Water in 2017 more than once and was intrigued by its premise. The year is 1962. The city is Baltimore. The setting, in great part, a sterile, damp, underground government lab where something arrives, called an “asset,” and is kept in a water tank/aquarium. One of the night crew cleaning ladies, Elisa (Sally Hawkins), a plain, mute woman, who, because of her lack of speech is, while friendly, also timid and deeply lonely; yet, atypically, finds she is compelled to explore what is in the tank. To her surprise what she discovers is an amphibious humanoid creature (Doug Jones), covered in luminous scales, looking back at her with large liquid eyes. Captured in a river in the Amazon it is brought back by government agent Richard Strickland (Michael Shannon), a sadistic racist who takes pleasure in torturing the creature with an electric cattle prod and insists it is nothing more than an “abomination.” Strickland’s plan, actually an emphatic recommendation, is to kill the thing and dissect it in order to find anything that could be useful to the military and a bevy of scientists in their efforts to win the Cold War. And so ends act one. But director/writer Guillermo del Toro then takes the narrative in another direction and turns it into an adult fairy tale and love story in which Elisa develops a connection with the amphibian creature that is completely unexpected. She brings it hardboiled eggs, plays music on a portable phonograph, and teaches it rudimentary sign language. Thus begins a tale reminiscent of Beauty and the Beast, replete with scenes, balletic in their coupling, that convey a fearlessness, especially on the part of Elisa, as she expresses her desire (even lust) to consummate her feelings. Having learned about Strickland’s plan, she makes a courageous, life-altering choice. She refuses to yield, devises a plan, having felt no loneliness or isolation whenever with the creature. And so del Toro draws the audience deeper into his allegorical story. It is at this point that he asks the viewer to suspend his or her disbelief and accept what can seem a deeply improbable premise: a love story that is surreal. The question embedded in the relationship, which is beautifully rendered, is whether he asks too much. For some it will be a bridge too far, the fantasy stretching all credibility. Others will be swept away by the resonating contact between this silent woman and her need and an isolated creature conceived in the rich imagination of del Toro. (The amphibian humanoid does bring to mind the 1954 film, The Creature From the Black Lagoon.) I found that I couldn’t accept the core premise of the film and was not moved by Elisa’s reaching out to this strange man-fish. What I did take great pleasure in, however, was watching the stunning performance of Sally Hawkins, a consummate actress who starred in another deeply human film, Maudie, one in which she also faces overwhelming loneliness. She is amazing. But then so is the ensemble cast in The Shape of Water. Richard Jenkins and Michael Shannon are both superb. For me, however, it came down to the story, one that bears the signature of del Toro (Pan’s Labyrinth). His films are high risk, high gain for moviegoers. Yet I wouldn’t be surprised if The Shape of Water wins an Oscar for Best Picture (it has seven Golden Globe nominations) and Hawkins is nominated for Best Actress. I confess that it’s a bit disconcerting when a film is so fully embraced by critics and audiences and I find myself asking what I fail to see that for so many is both evocative and irresistible. But there it is. The Shape of Water. Directed by Guillermo del Toro. Starring Sally Hawkins, Richard Jenkins and Michael Shannon. 2 hrs., 3 min. Rated R.

articles.text: Jude Law as Dr. Watson and Robert Downey Jr. as Sherlock Holmes. Recall the image of Sherlock Holmes, made famous by Basil Rathbone who starred in some 14 movies featuring the English detective, always accompanied by Nigel Bruce who portrayed Dr. John Watson. Rathbone was long-faced, inscrutable, an ever-present Mahogany Calabash pipe with a meerschaum bowl, and, of course, his signature deerstalker cap, a checked twill, double-brimmed lid that was soon identified as a detective’s hat. Those films, shot from 1939 to 1946, were inspired by the works of Sir Arthur Conan Doyle who preceded English mystery writers such as Agatha Christie, P.D. James and Ngalo Marsh, and who created a panoply of studied whodunits involving the butler in the library with the candlestick, so to speak. Rathbone’s Holmes – always careful and deliberative, never given to emotional outbursts or physical confrontations – has likely shaped the expectations of many moviegoers who turned out to see the more contemporaneous Sherlock Holmes. They are in for a treat. The newly reconstructed Holmes is no longer a detective of the ilk of Agatha Christie’s Miss Marple or Hercule Poirot. Robert Downey’s Holmes is a rogue, dissolute, a master of martial arts, athletic and courageous, given to dark rooms, extreme experiments, harrowing tight spots, a man so keenly observant, so completely aware of his surroundings that he is often tormented. As well, Jude Law’s Dr. Watson has been nicely revisited. No longer is he the bumbling foil; rather, he’s as capable – intellectually and physically – as is Holmes. When together, which is often, they bicker and disagree and yet have been friends for years. So much does Holmes need Watson’s assistance that he is willing to undermine Watson’s pending marriage. This new Holmes is a surprise and far more interesting than any of Holmes’ antecedents, making the film engaging. However, at the center of every Holmes narrative is a mystery: the essential whodunit. And here the screenwriters stumble. Rather than writing a tale that will keep the audience guessing, the villain, Lord Blackwood (Mark Strong), is revealed at the outset, and so it’s never a question of who but how. This Holmes becomes a howdunit, not quite as compelling as a whodunit. Still, the film is rich with close calls for Holmes and Watson as well as Irene Adler (Rachel McAdams), the one woman in Holmes’ life who continues to interest him with her courage, intelligence and insouciance. Suffice it to say that Holmes, in this incarnation, is a man of action as well as a man of incisive deductive reasoning, making for a solidly entertaining movie. Sherlock Holmes. Starring Robert Downey, Jude Law, Rachel McAdams and Eddie Marsan. Directed by Guy Ritchie. 2 hrs., 8 min. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: Sherlock Holmes a fine update with Robert Downey

articles.text: Onward, released by Pixar and Disney, brings to bear once again what has proved to be a marvelous engine of imagination that creates, with each film, a special world that beckons kids of all ages to enter and enjoy. The world created in Onward is one of blue-toned elves who live in toadstool houses, a place of dragons, unicorns, magic, spells – and not to forget some engaging wizardry. From the outset, the story is carried by two brothers: shy Ian (Tom Holland), who has just turned 16, and the older Barley (Chris Pratt), a tad different and rebellious. They are the Lightfoot brothers and a study in contrasts. They discover a birthday gift left to Ian by his deceased dad: it’s a wizard’s staff, a rare phoenix gem, and a letter of instructions that will allow their dad to return for just one day. Of course, Ian, with Barley’s help, makes a valiant attempt and only manages to get half-way through the spell, resulting in dad ending up as a pair of pants, socks and shoes. What is needed is a new gemstone to replace the one that fizzled. Barley is certain he knows where to find one. And so the adventure begins. The bros set out on a quest that will take them from place to place, each fraught with obstacles and perilous moments. The part of this hunt that is special is that they take half their dad along, hooked up to a doggy leash so he can’t wander off. Dad, after all, can’t speak or see, hence is what we might describe as high maintenance. Their mode of transportation is Barley’s well-used van, outfitted with some amazing stuff, like blasting air conditioning. Of course the bros bicker about directions, and the ability of Ian to use the staff to create critical magic when needed. What is surprising is that there is a tone of sadness to the story. The bros both are grieving for their dad. Born shortly after his dad died, Ian never knew their father. Barley, however, does have small kid memories and yearns for more. They are convinced once they locate the special stone they will complete their dad’s final transformation and have that one very special day they both hope for. So, onward. There are lots of speed bumps along the way, hence the film is essentially episodic, comedic, and situational. And for good measure, their mom, Laurel (Julia Louis-Dreyfus), is right behind them, certain they are in danger. It’s all in the Pixar wheelhouse, and kids ages six to eight will enjoy the journey and the cast of characters, even ColtBronco, a centaur police officer (Mel Rodriquez), and a strange restaurant, replete with a Manticore (Octavia Spencer). That’s where they find a much needed map to help them find their way on their journey. It’s all a trip to be enjoyed, especially if you’re a kid (or a parent) and relish quality time in elf-land. Onward. Directed by Dan Scanlon. Pixar-Disney animation. With voices of Chris Pratt, Tom Holland, Octavia Spencer and Julia Louis-Dreyfus. 1 hr., 54 min. Rated PG

articles.text: Eric Clapton was raised by his grandparents. When his grandfather Jack Clapp found out Eric had been dropped from the Kingston School of Art after skipping classes to play guitar and drink in local pubs, he gave him an ultimatum: “Work with me or get out of the house”. Jack Clapp was a master plasterer, master bricklayer and master carpenter. The work discipline his grandfather emulated was appreciated by Eric and seems to have set a similar standard in his music. No matter what was going on in life, he has always gone to great lengths to prepare styles and pieces for performances and recordings. There aren’t many “bad notes” in EC’s playing. African-American field hollers and work songs have indirectly been a resource for Clapton. They are the source of the 12-bar blues chord progressions and the core melodies for blues. EC particularly studied Robert Johnson and Big Bill Broonzy. He incorporated rhythms from the black fife and drum tradition and from “rival rhythms”. Those rhythms were developed by slaves using Revolutionary War and Civil War instruments and rudimentary drum rhythms, blended with African rhythm. English rock and blues guitar master Eric Clapton. Here are links to my related playlists on Spotify: http://www. guitarimprov.com/FieldHollers. pdf Clapton’s blues style example 1 is based on sixteenths (four notes per beat), Robert Johnson’s style, fife and drum rhythms and revival rhythms. Clapton’s blues style example 2 is an up-tempo triple-time (three notes per beat) blues style that Clapton adapted from Freddie King and B.B. King. Links to notation and live guitar audio are provided near the end of this column. The British blues revival in the sixties was the backdrop for EC’s blues guitar development. He quit the Yardbirds in 1965 because they moved from blues rock to pop rock. He joined John Mayall and the Bluesbreakers, his friend Jimmy Page recommended Jeff Beck as a replacement. While working on the great Bluesbreakers album with bandleader John Mayall, EC was being paid to work eight hours a day on the album. On one of the recording days when they finished well before eight hours, EC asked, “Mr. Mayall, what should I do in the remaining time?” Mayall answered, “Go practice”. He did practice. Eric Clapton was influenced by Robert Johnson, Freddie King, B.B. King, Albert King, and Muddy Waters. He in turn influenced most current blues rock guitarists, including Eddie Van Halen, who influenced Joe Satriani. The roots of the electric blues guitar tradition is now thankfully kept alive by Joe Bonamassa, a great admirer of Clapton. It cuts back and forth between the tale of Ailey Pearl Garfield, a Black girl growing up at the end of the 20th century, and the “songs” of her ancestors, Native Americans and enslaved African Americans. ful account of the struggle to reconcile art and life. Yet for all the dramatic twists of her life, these books together project a stunning clarity, humor and candidness. How the Word Is Passed: A Reckoning with the History of Slavery Across America, by Clint Smith. Little, Brown & Company. For this timely and thought-provoking book, Smith, a poet and journalist, toured sites key to the history of slavery and its present-day legacy. Smith holds up a mirror to America’s fraught relationship with its past, capturing a potent mixture of good intentions, earnest corrective, willful ignorance and blatant distortion. Invisible Child: Poverty, Survival and Hope in an American City, by Andrea Elliott. Random House. The book expands on her acclaimed 2013 series for “The Times” about Dasani Coates, a homeless New York schoolgirl, and her family. Elliott spent years following her subjects in their daily lives, through shelters, schools, courtrooms and welfare offices. The book is a searing account of one family’s struggle with poverty, homelessness and addiction. How Beautiful We Were, by Imbolo Mbue, Random House. Mbue’s sweeping and quietly devastating second novel begins in 1980 in the fictional African village of Kosawa, where representatives from an American oil company have come to meet with the locals, whose children are dying because of the environmental havoc (fallow fields, poisoned water) wreaked by its drilling and pipelines. Through the eyes of Kosawa’s citizens young and old, Mbue constructs a nuanced exploration of self-interest, of what it means to want in the age of capitalism and colonialism. Intimacies, by Katie Kitamura, Riverhead Books. In Kitamura’s fourth novel, an unnamed court translator in The Hague is tasked with intimately vanishing into the voices and stories of war criminals whom she alone can communicate with; falling meanwhile into a tumultuous entanglement with a man whose marriage may or may not be over for good. Kitamura’s sleek and spare prose elegantly breaks grammatical convention. No One Is Talking About This, by Patricia Lockwood. Riverhead Books. Lockwood first found acclaim as a poet on the internet, with gloriously inventive and ribald verse. Here, in her first novel, she distills the pleasures and deprivations of life split between online and flesh-and-blood interactions, transfiguring the dissonance into art. The result is a book that reads like a prose poem, at once sublime, profane, intimate, philosophical, hilarious and, eventually, deeply moving. When We Cease to Understand the World, by Benjamín Labatut. Translated by Adrian Nathan West. New York Review Books. Labatut expertly stitches together the stories of the 20th century’s greatest thinkers to explore both the ecstasy and agony of scientific breakthroughs: their immense gains for society as well as their steep human costs. His journey to the outermost edges of knowledge offers glimpses of a universe with limitless potential underlying the observable world. The Love Songs of W.E.B. DuBois, by Honorée Fanonne Jeffers. Harper/HarperCollins The first novel by Jeffers, a celebrated poet, is many things at once: a moving coming-ofOn Juneteenth, by Annette Gordon-Reed. Liveright Publishing. Exploring the racial and social complexities of Texas, her home state, Gordon-Reed asks readers to step back from the current heated debates and take a more nuanced look at history. Such a perspective comes easy to her because she was a part of history – the first Black child to integrate her East Texas school. On several occasions, she found herself shunned by whites and Blacks alike, learning at an early age that breaking the color line can be threatening to both races. Red Comet: The Short Life and Blazing Art of Sylvia Plath, by Heather Clark. Alfred A. Knopf. It’s daring to undertake a new biography of Plath, whose life, and death by suicide at 30 in 1963, have been thoroughly picked over by scholars. Determined to rescue the poet from posthumous caricature as a doomed madwoman and Clark aims to “reposition her as one of the most important American writers of the 20th century.” Clark, a professor of poetry in England, delivers a transporting account of a rare literary talent enlivened throughout by quotations from Plath’s letters, diaries, poetry and prose.

Here, in her first novel, she distills the pleasures and deprivations of life split between online and flesh-and-blood interactions, transfiguring the dissonance into art. The result is a book that reads like a prose poem, at once sublime, profane, intimate, philosophical, hilarious and, eventually, deeply moving. When We Cease to Understand the World, by Benjamín Labatut. Translated by Adrian Nathan West. New York Review Books. Labatut expertly stitches together the stories of the 20th century’s greatest thinkers to explore both the ecstasy and agony of scientific breakthroughs: their immense gains for society as well as their steep human costs. Translated by Tiina Nunnally and Michael Favala Goldman. Farrar, Straus & Giroux. Ditlevsen’s gorgeous memoirs, first published in Denmark in the 1960s and ’70s and collected here in a single volume, detail her hardscrabble upbringing, career path and merciless addictions: a powerOn Juneteenth, by Annette Gordon-Reed. Liveright Publishing. Exploring the racial and social complexities of Texas, her home state, Gordon-Reed asks readers to step back from the current heated debates and take a more nuanced look at history. Such a perspective comes easy to her because she was a part of history – the first Black child to integrate her East Texas school. articles.text: The winter season is upon us, bringing shorter days, a new wave of COVID-19 cases, and much needed rain and storms to the region. The cooler winter months also occasionally bring poor air quality conditions to the Bay Area, often caused by particulate matter pollution (e.g., wood smoke) that gets trapped close to the ground by an inversion layer (i.e., a layer of warm air above cooler air near the Earth’s surface). Worsening the air quality is the use of gasoline-powered landscape maintenance equipment such as leaf blowers and lawn mowers. This equipment is driven by small off-road engines (SORE), spark-ignition engines rated below 19 kilowatts. According to the California Air Resources Board, the number of SOREs in California (16.7 million) is greater than that of light-duty passenger cars (13.7 million) and is overwhelmingly comprised of residential lawn and garden equipment (77%). The emissions from these small engines are significant. The best-selling commercial leaf blower, during one hour of operation, emits smog-forming pollution comparable to driving a 2017 Toyota Camry about 1100 miles, or approximately the distance from Los Angeles to Denver. In fact, SOREs are on pace to produce more pollution each year than passenger cars. This can be attributed to regulations on car exhaust getting more restrictive over the years, and thus substantially reducing their ozone-damaging emissions. But the same cannot be said for SOREs. Gas-powered leaf blowers expose workers and the public to high levels of toxic and carcinogenic emissions such as formaldehyde, benzene, and particulate matter in equipment fumes, wreaking havoc on local air quality and causing unsafe levels of noise. Across the U.S., hundreds of cities and counties have passed laws restricting or prohibiting the use of gas-powered leaf blowers. Piedmont was the first city in the East Bay and one of the first in California to ban the use of gas-powered leaf blowers, in 1990. Starting as early as 2024, the state of California will outlaw the sale of new gas-powered leaf blowers, lawn mowers, and chain saws. The good news is that electric and battery-powered leaf blowers are simple, light, easy to use, reliable and the cost is decreasing. No more running out of gas, replacing old spark plugs, or cumbersome and heavy equipment. All you need to do is insert a charged battery, flip the switch, and get to work. Lower maintenance costs also mean electric leaf blowers will save you money in the long run. Learn more information about Piedmont’s leaf blower regulations here: https://www.piedmont. ca.gov/services___departments/ public_works/sustainability_division/leaf_blower_regulations. Alyssa Dykman is the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Program Manager. She can be reached at adykman@piedmont. ca.gov.

Orange-Scented Olive Oil Cake Adapted from Cook’s Illustrated INGREDIENTS • 1 3/4 cups all-purpose flour • 1 teaspoon baking powder • 3/4 teaspoon table salt • 3 extra-large eggs, room temperature • 1 cup granulated sugar, plus 1 tablespoon to sprinkle atop before baking • 1 teaspoon orange zest, finely grated (I use a Microplane for grating) • 3/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil • 1/2 cup whole milk, room temperature • 1/4 cup orange juice, freshly squeezed after removing the zest, room temperature INSTRUCTIONS Position an oven rack to the mid-oven position and preheat the oven to 350°F. Oil the bottom and sides of a 9-inch round springform pan. A regular 9-inch round cake pan will work too. Line the bottom with parchment and turn it top side up when you remove the cake from the pan to complete cooling. Whisk flour, baking powder, and salt together in a medium bowl. Set aside. Combine the milk and orange juice. Set aside. Using a handheld electric mixer, beat the eggs on medium speed until foamy, about 1 minute. Add 1 cup of sugar and orange zest, and whip on high speed until the mixture is fluffy and pale yellow, about 2 minutes. Reduce speed to medium, and while mixer is running, pour the olive oil in a slow, steady stream. Mix until oil is fully incorporated. On low speed, add half of the flour mixture and mix until barely incorporated. Stop to scrape the sides and bottom of the bowl if needed. Add the milk-orange juice mixture and mix until combined. Add remaining flour mixture and mix until just incorporated. Scrape down the bowl as needed. Be careful to not over mix. Pour the batter into the prepared pan and sprinkle the remaining 1 tablespoon of granulated sugar evenly over the entire surface. Bake until the cake is deep golden brown, about 40–45 minutes. Test for doneness by inserting a toothpick in the center of the cake. It should come out with only a few crumbs clinging. Transfer the pan to a wire rack and cool for 15 minutes. Remove the sides of the springform pan and cool completely before serving. Note: The cake needs no further adornment as the granulated sugar sprinkled on top forms a lovely sparkle and crunch. I decorated my cake with candied orange rind, some dipped in chocolate to fancy it up. This is totally optional. articles.text: Photos by Kate Fratar The doorway to City of London Distillery sits below the steeple of St. Bride’s Church, known as the church of the media and press, and just off Fleet Street, once home to a bustling newspaper scene. Aboard the Flying Scotsman – a train, lest the name suggest otherwise – I’m bound for Edinburgh and the second stop on this summer’s spirits trail. The primary focus of this adventure will be on whisky tasting and studying the subtleties of peat and esters. The kickoff to this hard-nosing jaunt came in London, where the emphasis was on gins. Because, well, when in Rome, as they say. Tucked away on an easily missed side alley of Fleet Street is the City of London Distillery. Founded in 2012, the urban upstart is bringing back the tradition of gin distillation to the City of London after a nearly 200-year absence. During the eighteenth century, gin distilleries sprouted in this area, originally the site of a fortified Roman settlement at Londonium, as citrus fruits became available through London’s port. Among the distillery’s gins, The Square Mile is a nod to the two square miles that establishes the City of London as a separate entity, complete with its own mayor and independent police force, within the jurisdiction of Greater London. Its doorway sits beneath the steeple of St. Bride’s Church, known as the church of the media and the press. Down the narrow wooden stairs is the bottle shop, bar, tasting room, and fireproofed, glassed-walled distillery. The cozy setup, complete with dark green paint and plush leather chairs, echoes an era when cigarette smoke might have lingered overhead and the din of clacking typewriters would have overridden conversation (perhaps of the latest news tip?). It’s one-part speakeasy to two-parts journalist hideaway. Jake meets me to host a tour – including the botanicals room, where guests can tinker with their own blends of spices and take the concoction home – and a tasting. The four pillars of the City of London production line are all in the classic London Dry style, with varying levels of citrus. There are also gins infused with rhubarb, lemon and mandarin, respectively, made more as experiments to play within market trends. The City of London Authentic gin won a Double-Gold Award at the San Francisco World Spirits Competition in 2017. The recognition is when the distillery decided to stop any further finessing of the recipe, Jake noted. In 2016, the Christopher Wren, named for the architect of St. Paul’s Cathedral, the more recognizable church-top to overlook the distillery, took home the same award. Where the Christopher Wren carries more undertones of orange, the citrus lacing the Old Tom is primarily lemon zest. The garnishes of orange twist with Christopher Wren and lemon with hibiscus for the Old Tom, along with the choice of tonic, bring variation to the standard G&T on the bar menu. It was a different classic gin cocktail that I wanted to see sampled, however. The Florentine invention turns 100 years old this year. In 2018, it was the second-most ordered cocktail worldwide, according to a poll conducted by the magazine Drinks International of more than 100 bars. articles.text: Longtime Piedmont resident Marian Smith died on January 26. She was 86. Marian Bamford Smith of Piedmont, California, died January 26, 2022 at home at the age of 86. Her husband, Harold Smith, said she passed away peacefully after a brief illness. Born in North Andover, Massachusetts in 1935, Marian was the eldest of nine children of H. Russell and Marie (Theroux) Bamford. She attended Johnson High School, received a B.S. degree in Physics from Simmons College in 1956, was a graduate student in the Department of Metallurgy at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology from 1957-59, and received an MBA degree in finance from the Haas School of Business, University of California, Berkeley in 1982. Until 1966, Marian worked as a research scientist at Raytheon, at the Ballistics Research Laboratories at the Aberdeen Proving Grounds, and at UC Berkeley. For the next 14 years, she concentrated on raising her children who were active junior tennis players and who played for their college tennis teams (two at Harvard, one at Yale). While the children were in college, Marian was a full-time student at the University of California (Berkeley) Haas School of Business. Until retirement in 2005, Marian was a principal of the Palmer Smith Corporation, an aerospace management consulting firm. She was appointed trustee of the Board of the Alameda County Employees’ Retirement Association (ACERA) in 1989. She was the first woman to chair the ACERA Board as well as the first woman to chair the ACERA Investment Committee. She was a member of the Executive Board of the Council of Institutional Investors, the Smithsonian Institution Investment Committee, and the Stanford Law School Fiduciary Education Advisory Board. An active genealogist and writer, she documented French and French Canadian ancestors back to 1625 and English ancestors back to 1835. She was a 10th generation descendant of Antoine Terroux who arrived in Quebec in 1693 from Verdun-sur-Garonne. Her ancestor, Augustin Hebert, one of the first colonists of Montreal, emigrated from Caen in France in 1641. Her Bamford and Latham English ancestors emigrated from Rochdale, England in the 1870s to work in the textile mills of North Andover, Massachusetts. A regular golf and tennis player, she was a member of the Claremont Country Club and the Berkeley Tennis Club. Marian and Harold lived an active and eventful life together with many fond memories including a river rafting trip through the Grand Canyon where the attached photo was taken. Marian is survived by her husband, Dr. Harold P. Smith, Jr. of Piedmont, daughters Natalya Marie Smith of La Jolla, and Erika Bamford Smith of Oakland, and son Harold (Peter) P. Smith, III and his wife Patricia McCoy Smith of Oakland. She is also survived by grandchildren Andrew Smith of Oakland, and Harold Gonzalez and Natasha Gonzalez of La Jolla. She is additionally survived by her sisters Roberta Banan of Longboat Key, Florida, and Jacqueline (John) Moran of Little Compton, Rhode Island, and her brothers, Gilbert (Gail) Bamford of Vero Beach, Florida, David Bamford of Sarasota, Florida and James Bamford of Andover, Massachusetts. She is predeceased by her siblings Edith Welch of Longboat Key, Florida, and Susan Sullivan and Stephan Bamford of Andover, Massachusetts. Burial services will be private. A celebration of Marian’s life will be held at an appropriate time.
